result:
The town kept its lost things in a room beneath the swimming pool.

Most were ordinary: goggles, towels, a single shoe that had been waiting so long its owner was surely old enough to vote. But behind a locked door, on shelves made damp by the pool above, were the things people didn’t know they had lost until someone handed them back.

A man once came in for his umbrella and left with the memory of his mother singing while she peeled potatoes. He sat on the curb outside for twenty minutes, holding the umbrella closed in the rain.

I worked there on Tuesdays.

My job was to label the items. This was harder than it sounds. Courage, for instance, came in many forms: a small brass button, a warm stone, a letter with no address. Patience was usually a spool of thread, though once it arrived as a sleeping moth.

The room had rules. We couldn’t advertise. We couldn’t keep anything for ourselves. And we couldn’t return an item unless its owner asked for it, even if they didn’t know quite what they were asking for.

“What am I looking for?” people would say.

“That depends,” I’d tell them. “What have you tried?”

One Tuesday, a girl came down the stairs carrying a paper bag. She was perhaps twelve, with wet hair and a swimming medal knocking against her zipper.

“I think you have something of mine,” she said.

“What is it?”

“I don’t know. My dad says I used to be funny.”

I asked her to wait. In the back room I found a jar full of laughter, a packet of riddles, and a wind-up duck that marched in circles. None had her name on it. On the bottom shelf, though, was a small red mitten. Its label read: **THE ABILITY TO BE SILLY WITHOUT FEELING WATCHED.**

“Is that it?” she asked when I brought it out.

“I think so.”

She put it on. It was too small, but she worked her fingers in anyway.

“Nothing’s happening.”

“Maybe you have to try it somewhere else.”

She looked disappointed, but she thanked me and left the medal on the counter by mistake. I ran upstairs after her and found her in the lobby, standing in front of the vending machine.

I held out the medal. She took it, then glanced at her reflection in the glass. Wearing one red mitten and one bare hand, she made the mitten wave at her.

She looked around to see if anyone was watching.

I pretended to examine the price of crisps.

After a moment, she made the mitten wave again, this time with its thumb tucked in, like a tiny person bowing. Then she laughed, just once, and went out to meet her father.

Downstairs, I wrote **RETURNED** on the label and put it in the empty jar.
